cases.name: an activity call commits one scheduled activity, and its completion closes the run
a later command is appended past an unconsumed completion (hot execution)
the same commits come out of a cold replay in one-event chunks
a signal that arrives first wins the select, and the losing timer wait is cancelled

differences.what: The command sequence number a `select` allocates for itself, and everything downstream of it. Rust's select! macro reserves the select's own command id BEFORE polling any branch, so a two-branch select numbers select=1, branch=2, branch=3. TypeScript's select allocates it inside resolveSelectWinner, which runs only once a branch is ready, so the same select numbers branch=1, branch=2, select=3 — and in a task where no branch is ready it allocates nothing at all. The shift moves every branch's command seq by one, which is why it also shows up in wait command ids, in the command ids of the waits a losing branch's cancellation deletes, and in the activity id, which is formatted from the command id. Both numberings are internally consistent and both replay against their own histories, but the numbering is durable: a history written by one runtime cannot be replayed by the other. Recorded from both sides rather than normalised away, because this is a convergence decision — which runtime moves — and not a language-forced difference. It is the last one left: every other divergence this corpus recorded has been closed by moving TypeScript onto Rust's answer.

cases.name: a query projection is committed with the signal wait and again with its consumption
a child workflow start is committed to the outbox and its completion closes the parent
an activity map commits one scheduled map bounded by maxInFlight
a version marker, a side effect and a deprecated patch land in one commit with the result
continue-as-new commits the next run's input and nothing else
a timer scheduled after the clock has moved records its deadline relative to now

declaredGaps.why: A three-way split, not a two-way one. Rust's ActivityHandle::result(self) takes self by value, so a second await does not compile at all. Rust's ChildWorkflowHandle::result(&self) borrows, so both a second concurrent await and a second sequential read compile — and take_child_completion removes the entry from the index, so the second await returns Poll::Pending forever and the workflow silently stalls. TypeScript allows a sequential re-read and rejects a concurrent one. Three behaviours across two runtimes and two handle kinds; no corpus case awaits a handle twice. No corpus case awaits a handle twice, so this is a gap rather than a projection: there is nothing here for the runners to normalise, only behaviour nobody looked at.

Every payload in every case is inline. payload_json/payloadJson call decode_payload/decodePayload, which refuse a Blob ref, so a case that started offloading would fail loudly rather than under-assert — but nothing exercises the payload-offload layer, its digest/size/uri fields, or the hydration a provider must perform before replay. The corpus says nothing about offloaded payload parity in either direction.

No case schedules one. commit_json and commitJson both refuse a commit whose scheduleChildWorkflowMaps is non-empty, so this cannot be reached accidentally, but the ChildWorkflowMapScheduled event, the ChildWorkflowMapTask, and the child-map result manifest have no behavioural coverage here. The Phase 6 map transition table covers the engine; this covers neither the scheduling commit nor the completion commit.

Every case completes successfully or continues as new. WorkflowFailed, WorkflowCancelled and the failure payloads they carry have neutral encoders in both runners but no case that produces them, so the encoders themselves are untested. The coverage test's exact-union assertion over event kinds is what will force this list to be updated the day a case does produce one.

Every activity in the catalogue succeeds on its first attempt, so the corpus never observes a second attempt, a retry delay, or an ActivityTimedOut. That is partly deliberate — retry delay VALUES are a forced divergence and are excluded above — but the shape of a retry (attempt number, whether a new task is scheduled at all) is comparable and is not compared.

The plan calls this out as one of the behaviours a vocabulary fixture cannot pin, and it is still not pinned. No case drives a workflow to a terminal event while a command event remains unconsumed at the replay cursor, so neither runtime's detection of that condition is compared against the other's.

declaredGaps.what: The select tie-break between two branches ready at the same event id
declaredGaps.why: There are TWO implementations of the rule in Rust, not one: the select! macro expands its own comparison (durust-macros/src/lib.rs) and select_all carries a separate copy (src/runtime.rs). TypeScript has compareSelectReadyBranches. All three order ready branches by ready event id and then by branch ordinal. The event-id half is pinned for the macro path and for TypeScript by the two-ready-branch cases, in both orders, and reversing either implementation fails them. What this corpus does NOT pin: the select_all copy, which no case reaches — pre-existing replay_core tests do cover it, so it is untested by the corpus rather than untested outright — and the ordinal half of the rule, for any implementation. The ordinal half appears unreachable through the public API: every ready branch resolves from a distinct history event — a TimerFired, an activity completion, or the SignalConsumed the task is about to append — so two ready branches cannot share a ready event id, and a comparator reading 'lowest event id, then HIGHEST ordinal' passes both cases here. It is recorded as a gap rather than claimed as an assertion, because a future change that let two branches share an event id would land on untested code.

declaredGaps.what: Providers other than the two in-memory ones
declaredGaps.why: Every case runs against MemoryBackend. That is less single-provider than it sounds — Rust and TypeScript have entirely independent MemoryBackend implementations, so the corpus is implicitly cross-checking two providers as well as two runtimes — but neither SQLite nor Postgres executes a single corpus case in either language, and provider-specific commit handling is covered only by the separate conformance suites.

exclusions.why: Rust hashes std::any::type_name::<T>(); TypeScript hashes a SchemaAdapter fingerprint, or the literal string "unknown" when no adapter is supplied. Neither derivation can produce the other's value for the same logical payload, and there is no API on the Rust side that lets a caller override it. Every payload in this corpus is therefore projected to {codec, schemaFingerprint: "<schema-fingerprint>", value: <decoded>}: the codec and the decoded content are asserted, the fingerprint is not.

exclusions.what: CommandFingerprint.optionsDigest for the Activity and ActivityMap kinds
exclusions.why: Rust computes it as sha256(rmp_serde::to_vec_named(&ActivityOptions)) over snake_case field names with Duration encoded as {secs, nanos}; TypeScript computes sha256(JSON.stringify({taskQueue, retryPolicy, startToCloseTimeoutMs, heartbeatTimeoutMs})) over camelCase numbers. The two are different serialisations of different structs and can never agree. The options themselves are still asserted, field by field, on the ActivityScheduled/ActivityMapScheduled event and on the scheduled task. The Timer, Signal, ChildWorkflow, ChildWorkflowMap and VersionMarker option digests are plain formatted strings that do agree, and those are asserted for real.

exclusions.what: RetryPolicy beyond maxAttempts, including every retry delay value
exclusions.why: The two runtimes model retry differently and share no field but the attempt cap: Rust carries {backoff: None|Exponential, max_attempts}, TypeScript carries {initialIntervalMs, maxIntervalMs, maxAttempts, backoffCoefficient, nonRetryableErrorTypes}. There is no lossless mapping in either direction, so numeric parity is impossible rather than merely unmet, and the plan already records retry delay values as a forced divergence. maxAttempts is common to both and is asserted.

Rust's select! is positional and records the literal string "select:{n}" ("select_all:{n}" for select_all); TypeScript's select takes a named record and records sha256(JSON.stringify({kind: "select", branches: [...keys]})), over key names Rust's positional macro does not have. What the corpus asserts instead is the winner itself: branchOrdinal and winningEventId are compared exactly. That claim is only worth anything if some case resolves a select with MORE THAN ONE ready branch — with a single ready branch every comparator returns the same winner and the assertion cannot fail — so the corpus carries `a select resolved with two ready branches takes the lower ready event id`, in which the signal and the timer are both ready in the same task and the recorded winner is the one with the lower ready event id. Reversing either half of compareSelectReadyBranches fails that case. The ordinal half of the rule is a declared gap, not an assertion: see declaredGaps.

Rust formats a wait id as "{runId}:{seq}:timer" / "{runId}:{seq}:signal"; TypeScript formats the same wait as "{runId}:timer:{seq}" / "{runId}:signal:{seq}". The id is an opaque provider key within one store, so neither format is wrong, but they are not interchangeable and a store written by one runtime could not have its waits deleted by the other. The corpus asserts what the id stands for — kind plus command id — for both upserted and deleted waits, each runner parsing its own format back into that neutral triple. This is a real divergence discovered while building the corpus, not a language-forced one.

An input manifest is itself an encoded payload whose contents are nested PayloadRefs. Rust serialises {item_count, page_lengths, pages} in snake_case with an externally tagged PayloadRef ({"Inline": {...}}), TypeScript serialises {itemCount, pageLengths, pages} in camelCase with an internally tagged one ({"kind": "Inline", ...}), so the manifest bytes cannot match even when every item value does. The corpus asserts the manifest by content instead: item count, page lengths, and the decoded value of every item, each runner reading the manifest with its own decoder.

Both runtimes carry the field — cancel_commands in Rust, cancelCommands in TypeScript — both raise ParentCancelled from it, and both now write it from the same producer: a select branch that loses while still holding a scheduled activity, which Rust withdraws in ActivityFuture::__durust_cancel_branch and TypeScript in cancelActivityBranch. It stays excluded because no corpus case reaches that state — every select here races a timer against a signal, or races branches that have both already produced a value — and not because either runtime is unable to produce it. Both runners assert the field is empty on every recorded commit, so the first case that starts cancelling a command fails loudly in both languages instead of quietly asserting half a commit.

Rust polls futures and rebuilds a RuntimeContext per task; TypeScript keeps a long-lived hot promise chain (HotWorkflowExecution) and mutates its context in place through AsyncLocalStorage. Neither can adopt the other and the corpus does not try: it names no execution-internal state and asserts only the committed history and the provider contract. What it does assert is that the choice is unobservable through that contract — the hot/cold case pairs below run the same script with and without a cached execution and require byte-identical commits.

note: The shared BEHAVIOURAL corpus. One artefact, two runners:
tests/behavioral_corpus.rs and
typescript/packages/core/test/behavioral-corpus.test.ts.
core-events.json, provider-io.json and benchmark-output.json pin VOCABULARY:
event type names, fingerprint helpers, payload-ref shapes, provider request
and outcome names. Two runtimes can agree on every one of those and still
disagree about what a workflow task DOES. This file pins that. Each case is
(workflow program, input history, live signals, now) -> commit, and both
runtimes must reproduce the commit by executing the case through their real
worker, with the commit captured by a recording provider rather than rebuilt
from runtime state.
SCHEMA
`program`   names an entry in a catalogue that exists once per language
with the same observable behaviour. The corpus never carries
code.
`steps`     are provider-level actions — run a workflow task, run an
activity, advance the virtual clock, fire due timers, send a
signal, restart the worker with a given replay chunk size — so
the input history is produced the same way on both sides.
`historyBefore` pins that input history as literal data, read from the
provider immediately before the task is claimed.
`expect`    is the neutral projection of the WorkflowTaskCommit, asserted
by BOTH runners.
`divergence` replaces `expect` where the two runtimes genuinely behave
differently. It holds `what` (why they differ and which way the
convergence should go) plus BOTH observed commits, `rust` and
`typescript`; each runner asserts its own side. Recording both
is the point: a divergence that is normalised away stops being
visible, and one that is merely omitted stops being tracked.
Both runners refuse a divergence whose two sides are equal.
The two diff implementations agree on every structural shape —
nested objects, arrays of differing length, null against an
absent key, object against scalar, key ordering, deep key-set
mismatch — and disagree on exactly one class: numeric
REPRESENTATION. Rust compares serde_json::Number, which
distinguishes 1.0 from 1, -0.0 from 0, and 9007199254740993
from 9007199254740992; TypeScript compares JSON.stringify after
JSON.parse has already collapsed each of those pairs, so it
reports no difference. Rust's path set is therefore a superset
in every disagreement, which is why this cannot fail silently:
declare the extra path and TypeScript rejects it as spurious,
omit it and Rust rejects the omission. One runner always goes
red, and check:fixtures and CI both run both. Unreachable
today — every number in every commit is an integer inside the
double-safe range — so it is recorded rather than fixed.
`exclusions` are the projections `expect` applies before comparing, each
with the reason it cannot be compared directly. Both runners
assert the exclusion list itself, in order, so an exclusion
cannot be quietly widened or dropped.
`workerStartJitter` is not a commit; see its own note.
AUTHORING
The `expect` blocks were produced by the Rust runner under
DURUST_CORPUS_REGENERATE=1 and are checked in. The TypeScript runner has no
regeneration path at all: it can satisfy the file or fail. That asymmetry
is what makes the corpus a cross-implementation assertion rather than a
snapshot of one implementation — every shared `expect` here is a value one
runtime produced and the other had to match without having seen it.
DURUST_CORPUS_PRINT=1 makes the TypeScript runner report what it observed,
for filling in a `divergence.typescript` block; it never writes this file.
FOUND WHILE BUILDING THIS
Four differences turned up that nothing had recorded before. Three have
since been closed by moving TypeScript onto Rust's answer, and each entry
below keeps what the corpus saw as well as where it landed, because a
finding that leaves no trace once it is fixed cannot be audited.
1. TypeScript never cancelled a losing select branch's operational state.
CLOSED. It was recorded as a `divergence` on the two select-resolution
steps whose `deleteWaits` lengths differed, with the observable
consequence being a TimerFired appended after the terminal event.
TypeScript now cancels every branch that loses without producing a
value, so both runtimes delete the same waits, and those two steps
differ only by (2) below. The corpus reaches the timer and signal branch
kinds; the activity branch — which Rust withdraws through
`cancel_commands` rather than a wait — is not reached by any case here
and is covered by the `WorkflowTaskCommit.cancelCommands` exclusion.
2. A `select` allocates its own command sequence number before polling its
branches in Rust and after resolving a winner in TypeScript, which
shifts every branch's command seq by one. OPEN, and now the only
divergence this corpus records: it is a convergence decision about which
runtime moves, and until it is taken neither runtime can replay the
other's history across a select. Recorded as a `divergence` on every
step of every select case.
3. The TypeScript worker never supplied PrepareWorkflowTaskOptions.nowMs,
so a timer scheduled after the clock had moved recorded a deadline
measured from the epoch. CLOSED. `DurableBackend.currentTime()` now
exists in TypeScript as it always has in Rust, the worker reads it once
per prepared workflow task, and `a timer scheduled after the clock has
moved` is a shared expectation with both runtimes recording 6000. This
was an exclusion in the first draft, which was wrong: `fireAt` is
perfectly comparable, the runtimes simply differed, and an exclusion
would have hidden that behind a projection the runners do not perform.
4. WorkerOptions.activityTaskQueue in TypeScript was used only for CLAIMING
activity tasks — the worker never passed defaultActivityTaskQueue into
HotWorkflowExecution — so a callActivity() with no explicit taskQueue
scheduled onto the literal queue "default" and the worker that scheduled
it would never claim it. CLOSED, by giving the runtime the worker's
configured queue as its fallback exactly as Rust does. It could not be
expressed as a case at all: every program in this corpus names its task
queue explicitly, which is why the corpus ran green either way, and a
case that omitted the queue would be asserting a worker configuration
rather than a workflow behaviour.
The maintenance-scan jitter stream: FNV-1a-32 over the worker id's UTF-16
code units seeds mulberry32, and each call yields a unit value in [0, 1).
Verified identical across the two runtimes by hand during Phase 2 and
pinned here so nothing can drift.
`seed` is the FNV-1a-32 state before the first draw. `unitsScaled` are the
first six draws multiplied by 2^32 — that is, the raw 32-bit mulberry32
outputs, before the single exact division each runtime performs. Integers,
not decimals, deliberately: the division by 2^32 is exact in both runtimes,
so the integer form loses nothing, while decimal text does not survive the
round trip. serde_json parses 0.09126776782795787 to a double one ULP away
from what f64::from_str returns for the same text, which would have made a
decimal table fail in Rust for a reason that has nothing to do with jitter.
The DELAY these units are scaled into is NOT pinned: Rust keeps
sub-millisecond precision in a Duration, TypeScript rounds to whole
milliseconds. The stream is the shared part.
worker-🙂 is in the table on purpose: an astral character is two
UTF-16 code units and one four-byte UTF-8 sequence, so a runtime that
hashed bytes instead of code units would agree on every ASCII id here and
fail only on this one.
Rust asserts this table from src/worker.rs's unit tests, because
MaintenanceJitter is private to that module and a tests/ integration test
cannot name it; TypeScript asserts it from the corpus runner, which imports
the worker module directly.
